title: Islam: remembrance
hook: in the remembrance of God hearts find rest (Quran 13:28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat, the five daily prayers. Your line was five pauses. How many did you manage? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

Two in the morning, and a mind that won't stop. It replays the conversation from lunch, rehearses tomorrow's meeting, lists everything that could go wrong. Push the thoughts away and they come back louder. A few hours later, across town, an old man sits in a mosque after the dawn prayer, beads slipping through his fingers, lips moving softly, the same few words again and again. He looks rested. Today, on our visit to Islam: dhikr, remembrance.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, MIND RACING.` → `BEADS AFTER THE DAWN PRAYER.` → `DHIKR.`

segments.voice: Dhikr means remembrance, and also mention: to remember God, and to say God's name. The Qur'an asks for it often. Today's line, from surah thirteen, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Hearts find rest. Not by solving everything, but by remembering. Another verse turns it into a two-way street: remember me, God says, and I will remember you. The simplest dhikr is short phrases: subhanallah, glory be to God; alhamdulillah, praise be to God; Allahu akbar, God is greater. Hadith reports teach them after the daily prayers, thirty-three times each or close to it, counted on the fingers or on prayer beads called a misbaha or tasbih. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells that when Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was worn out from hard work and asked for a servant, he taught her to say these same phrases at bedtime, and said they were better for her than a servant. Dhikr can be silent or aloud, alone or together. Among Sufis, the mystical tradition within Islam, groups gather to chant God's names in rhythm, and some Sufi orders pair the words with the breath or with movement. Some keep a quiet dhikr going through the day: a phrase while waiting for the bus, while walking, while falling asleep. The idea is that the heart is always remembering something. Dhikr gives it something to remember that can hold its weight.
screen: `DHIKR — REMEMBRANCE, MENTION.` · `IN REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · `GLORY, PRAISE, GOD IS GREATER.` · `SILENT OR ALOUD, ALONE OR TOGETHER.` · then, large: `HEARTS FIND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one word slowly. Choose a word that settles you. If you're Muslim, it might be Allah, or alhamdulillah. If not, it can be peace, or here, or thank you. Breathe in. On the out-breath, say the word, silently or softly. Again. Again. When the mind runs off, don't scold it. Just return to the word. The bell holds the time.
Dhikr. Remembrance: short phrases said again and again, so that, as the Qur'an says, hearts find rest. Today's word.
Your line: hearts find rest. Tonight, if your mind starts racing, go back to your one word, and let it carry you toward sleep. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: After the daily prayers Muslims often say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar on their fingers or prayer beads, and Sufi communities gather for dhikr sessions of chanted remembrance.

fork.setup: Fatima is exhausted from hard work and asks her father for a servant. what does he give her?
options: a few phrases to say at bedtime.
fork.reveal: the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says he taught her subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar to say at bedtime, better for her than a servant.

trapdoor: what you thought: repeating words on beads.
what it means: remembering God through short phrases, so the heart can rest.
what a scholar hears: the root dh-k-r, remember and mention; Qur'an 13:28 and 2:152; the 'tasbih of Fatima' in Sahih al-Bukhari.
